paragraphs.heading: A ramp of sediment
paragraphs.text: The continental rise is a zone of gentle relief, made of piled-up sediment, lying between the continental slope and the abyssal plain. It is a major part of the continental margin and covers around 10% of the ocean floor. Its sediments are mostly silt and clay. Because it sits below the slope and is built by sediment settling out, it slopes very gently, usually between 1:50 and 1:500.

paragraphs.heading: How the sediment arrives
paragraphs.text: The rise grows as sediment is laid down, mostly through mass wasting, which is the downhill movement of sand and other sediment under gravity. Mass wasting can be slow, with sediment building up in fits and starts, or it can come in large, sudden events. The big ones are often set off by earthquakes or by the slope above becoming too steep. Slower build-up happens when hemipelagic sediment hanging in the seawater gradually sinks to the ocean basin.

paragraphs.heading: Fans at the foot of the slope
paragraphs.text: Where submarine canyons open out, sediment can heap up into enormous fan-shaped piles called submarine fans, on both the slope and the rise. These fans are shallow cone-shaped mounds at the base of the slope, and as neighbouring fans merge they form the continental rise. Canyons carved by erosion run downhill into fan valleys that get deeper as they go, and it is in this zone that the sediment of the rise is dropped.

paragraphs.heading: A giant example
paragraphs.text: The Bengal Fan stretches 3,000 kilometers and ranks among the largest sedimentary structures in the world. Many fans like it hold important oil and natural gas reservoirs. That makes them key spots for gathering seismic data.

paragraphs.heading: Out to the abyssal plain
paragraphs.text: Moving seaward, the sediment layers of the rise thin out and it blends into the abyssal plain, usually at a gradient of about 1:1000. The abyssal plain rests on basaltic oceanic crust and spans most of the seafloor. Its creatures are uniquely suited to the cold, the high pressure and the dark. Its flatness is broken by huge underwater mountain chains near the boundaries of Earth's tectonic plates.
